title: Synapse GoPro Worker
description: Read-only Matrix federation endpoints served by the GoPro worker: traffic, upstream latency, and shadow-mode agreement with Synapse.

list.name: bucket
list.label: Bucket
list.description: Range window for rate() and histogram_quantile(). 'auto' scales with the dashboard time range (minimum 30s). Prometheus scrapes this worker every 15s and rate() needs two samples in the window, so 5s/10s/15s return nothing at all and 30s is the practical floor. At this server's federation volume even 1m often reads as zero between requests, which is why the default is 5m.

panels.title: Request rate
panels.description: Federation requests served per second across all three endpoints.

panels.title: Failure ratio
panels.description: Share of requests returning 5xx. 502 means the upstream Synapse worker was unreachable, so a sustained non-zero value here is an availability problem, not a Matrix one.

panels.title: p99 upstream latency
panels.description: 99th percentile time waiting on Synapse. This is the baseline the native implementation has to beat.

panels.title: Upstream errors
panels.description: Rate of requests that could not reach any Synapse worker.

panels.title: Client disconnects
panels.description: Requests where the remote server hung up before we answered. Routine for slow /state calls; a spike suggests we became too slow for remote timeouts.

panels.title: Worker restarts
panels.description: Process starts recorded against the diff log, preserved across deploys.

panels.title: Request rate by endpoint
panels.description: /state and /state_ids are the expensive ones; /event is usually the most frequent.

panels.title: Upstream latency percentiles
panels.description: Time spent waiting on the Synapse worker, by endpoint. NOTE: this covers every request, including cancelled ones. To compare against the native implementation use the 'Native vs Synapse latency' panel, which measures both over the same requests.

panels.title: Status codes
panels.description: 403 is normal federation traffic (server not in room, or barred by a server ACL). 404 on /event is normal too. Watch for 502 and 'none'.

panels.title: Serving mode
panels.description: How each request was answered. During cutover this shows traffic shifting from proxy to native; a native fallback appears as proxy traffic on a native endpoint.

panels.title: Upstream latency distribution
panels.description: Full latency spread. Large rooms show up as a slow tail on /state.

panels.title: Response size percentiles
panels.description: /state on a large room returns megabytes of PDUs; this is what makes it costly.

panels.title: Overall match rate
panels.description: Agreement with Synapse across the whole run, restored from stats.json on restart. Empty until an endpoint is put into shadow mode.

panels.title: Comparisons
panels.description: Total shadow comparisons performed, cumulative across restarts.

panels.title: Mismatches
panels.description: Total disagreements. Must be zero, and stay zero for the soak window, before an endpoint is promoted.

panels.title: Time since last mismatch
panels.description: The promotion clock. It restarts every time the two implementations disagree. Green at 7 days.

panels.title: Dropped diff records
panels.description: Records lost because the writer queue was full. Any non-zero value means the diff log is incomplete and the promotion gate cannot be trusted.

panels.title: Diff log write errors
panels.description: Failures writing the log or its stats. Usually a full or read-only disk.

panels.title: Match rate by endpoint
panels.description: Endpoints are promoted individually, so each is tracked separately.

panels.title: Mismatch rate
panels.description: New disagreements per second. A flat zero line is what earns promotion.

panels.title: Native vs Synapse latency (same requests)
panels.description: The comparison the project exists to make. Both series cover ONLY the requests shadow comparison measured. Do not compare shadow_duration against gopro_upstream_duration_seconds: that one includes cancelled requests, which are skipped here and are by definition the slow ones, so it flatters the native implementation.

panels.title: Rejected (429)
panels.description: Requests refused outright. If this is non-zero while Synapse is not answering 429, our rc_federation is tighter than Synapse's and we are shedding load it would serve.

panels.title: Delayed
panels.description: Requests deliberately slowed rather than refused. Throttling starts here, well before any rejection, so this is the earlier warning of the two.

panels.title: Origins rejected
panels.description: Distinct servers rejected since startup. Answers whether throttling is one noisy server or many, which the counters alone cannot say.

panels.title: Servers tracked
panels.description: Origin servers with live limiter state. Also a rough count of who is talking to us.

panels.title: p99 limiter wait
panels.description: Latency the limiter itself adds. This is time we impose, not time we measure, so it is excluded from the native-vs-Synapse comparison.

panels.title: Rejection share
panels.description: Share of requests refused by the limiter.

panels.title: Rate limiting by endpoint
panels.description: Rejections and delays per endpoint. There is deliberately no per-origin series: this server has exchanged keys with tens of thousands of others, and a label per origin would be a cardinality explosion. Which server is being limited is in the worker logs, at warn for rejections and info for delays.

panels.title: Limiter wait time
panels.description: How long requests spend waiting on the limiter, by percentile.

panels.title: State group hit rate
panels.description: The one that matters. Resolving state at an event is by far the most expensive read; a state group's contents never change, so a hit turns a full recursive walk into a map lookup. Measured cold-vs-warm on the largest room here: 1.04s against 2us.

panels.title: Event hit rate
panels.description: Stored event JSON, which does not change.

panels.title: Cache memory
panels.description: Total across all caches. Compare against the configured bounds.

panels.title: Evictions
panels.description: Entries dropped to stay within the size bound. Sustained evictions on state_groups mean the bound is too small for the working set, and the expensive resolutions are being recomputed.

panels.title: Entries cached
panels.description: Total entries across all caches.

panels.title: Hit rate by cache
panels.description: Fraction of lookups served from memory, since startup. Caches are empty after a restart, so expect this to climb rather than start high.

panels.title: Cache size against bound
panels.description: Bytes held versus the configured limit. A cache pinned at its bound with steady evictions is undersized.

panels.title: Lookups per second
panels.description: Hits and misses by cache.

panels.title: Native latency against cache hit rate
panels.description: The point of the cache. Native p99 should fall as the state group hit rate rises.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: One process replacing N Python workers: goroutine count should track in-flight requests, not grow without bound.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Resident memory. The point of consolidating workers is a lower total than the Python fleet it replaces.

panels.title: GC pause
panels.description: Stop-the-world pause time. A large shared state cache shows up here first.
